title.en: Tailc son of Treon and the Woman of the World's Three Walks
title.zh: 特雷昂之子塔爾克與三繞世界之女

region.en: Hill of the Fianna's gathering, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭菲亞納集結之丘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VIII, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Dark clouds of blood hang over the Fianna's feats, and Finn's dream shows Aodh Beag headless and Goll fighting a very strong man. A beautiful woman with a crimson cloak comes asking protection from her husband Tailc son of Treon — skin of coal, the head and tail of a cat — and Finn gives it against the seven battalions. Thousands fall in their thousands; Osgar fights Tailc five days and nights without food or sleep and strikes his head off — and the woman, seeing all the slaughter done on account of her, falls dead of shame.
summary.zh: 菲亞納演武之際，血雲密佈，芬恩夢見無首的艾德·貝格與強人搏鬥的戈爾。一紅衣美婦前來求庇護，躲避其夫特雷昂之子塔爾克——他膚如煤炭、首尾若貓。芬恩以七營之力相保；千人千人的部隊潰滅；奧斯加與塔爾克晝夜五日無食無眠地血戰，終斬其首——而那女子見因己身而致的大屠殺，羞慚倒地而亡。

sensitivity.note: The blood-cloud omen and dream-oracle open the Book of the Fianna's wearing-away; the cat-headed marvel-man repeats the marvel-race repertoire (compare the Cat-Heads king slain by Abarthach). The heroine dying of shame at the rescue echoes Credhe's death for Cael — inversion of the grief-death. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One time the Fianna were all gathered together doing feats and casting stones, and the Druid of Teamhair that was with them said: "I am in dread, Finn of the Fianna, that there is some trouble near at hand; look now at those dark clouds of blood that are threatening us side by side overhead, and there is fear on me that there is some destruction coming on the Fianna." Finn lay down to sleep, and it was not long till he saw through his sleep Aodh Beag his son, and he without his head; and after that he saw Goll fighting with a very strong man. And then he heard a great shout, and saw Conan running, and the hounds after him; and when he came, Osgar asked him where was Aodh Beag. "Nothing troubles me but myself," said Conan; and Osgar found Aodh Beag with no fear or trouble on him at all, stopping there till he would hear the noise of the shields.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: They saw a great army coming as if in search of them, and a beautiful woman, having a crimson cloak, came to them over the plain, and her voice was as sweet as music: "I am the daughter of Garraidh, son of Dolar Dian, the Fierce; and my curse upon the King of Greece that bound me to the man that is following after me, and that I am going from, Tailc, son of Treon. For he has no good appearance, and his skin is of the colour of coal, and he has the head and the tail of a cat.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: And I have walked the world three times, and I did not leave a king or a great man without asking help from him, and I never got it yet." "I will give you protection, or the seven battalions of the Fianna will fall for your sake." A thousand of the Fianna went out to meet him and his men, and they all fell, and not one of them came back again; and another thousand of the best men of the Fianna, having blue and green shields, went out under Caoilte, son of Ronan, and they were worsted by Tailc and his people. Then Osgar asked leave of Finn to go out and fight the big man, and he himself and Tailc, son of Treon, were fighting through the length of five days and five nights without food or drink or sleep; and at the end of that time, Osgar made an end of Tailc, and struck his head off. And as to the young woman, when she saw all the slaughter that had been done on account of her, shame reddened her face, and she fell dead there and then.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. I; not verbatim.

region.en: Hill of the Fianna's gathering, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭菲亞納集結之丘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VIII, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: On the heels of Tailc's fall comes Meargach of the Green Spears, whose body no arms were ever reddened on, to avenge the queen-woman's death; Osgar fights him three days and at the last strikes off his head. Goll puts down Ciardan the Swift, and Conan — to Faolan's shame — takes Liagan the Nimble's head before the fight is begun: "If I could make an end of the whole army by one blow, I would do it, and I would not be ashamed."
summary.zh: 塔爾克既亡，梅爾加赫——「身經百戰而未嘗見血」的綠矛戰士——為王后之死而來復仇；奧斯加與其苦戰三日，終斬其首。戈爾誅「迅捷之基爾丹」；科南——令法奧蘭蒙羞——在交手之前便閃電般取下「敏捷之利亞根」首級：「若能一擊滅其全軍，我必為之而不以為恥。」

sensitivity.note: The honour-duel code (fair fight vs Conan's pragmatism) is debated in-text — a rare moment of the cycle commenting on its own ethics. Continuation record of the Tailc sequence; same symbolic pin.

passages.text: While the Fianna were gathered yet on the hill where Tailc, son of Treon, had been put down, they saw a very great champion coming towards them, having an army behind him; and he asked in a very rough voice where was Finn, the Head of the Fianna. "Meargach of the Green Spears is my name, and arms were never reddened yet on my body, and no one ever boasted of driving me backwards. Was it you, Finn, put down Tailc, son of Treon?" "It was not by me he fell, but by Osgar of the strong hand. And if it is satisfaction for her death or the death of Tailc you want, you can get it from a man of the Fianna, or you can go quietly from this place."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was Osgar stood up against him, and they fought a very hard fight through the length of three days, and at one time the Fianna thought it was Osgar was worsted, and they gave a great sorrowful shout. But in the end Osgar put down Meargach and struck his head off, and the army of Meargach keened him very sorrowfully. And after that, the two sons of Meargach, Ciardan the Swift and Liagan the Nimble, came up and asked who would come against them, hand to hand, that they might get satisfaction for their father.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: And it was Goll stood up against Ciardan, and it was not long till he put him down; and Conan came out against Liagan, and Liagan mocked at him: "It is foolishness your coming is, bald man!" But Conan made a quick blow and struck his head off before the fight was begun at all. And Faolan said that was a shameful thing to do, not to stand his ground and make a fair fight. But Conan said: "If I could make an end of the whole army by one blow, I would do it, and I would not be ashamed, and the whole of the Fianna could not shelter them from me."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Ailne of the Bright Face and her Keening of Omens
title.zh: 明顏之艾妮與兆象哀歌

region.en: Cnoc-an-Air (Hill of Slaughter), west of Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西部屠戮之丘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VIII, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: The battle stops on both sides for the coming of the golden-haired queen Ailne, who keens her husband Meargach and her two sons — and reads their deaths back through every omen: the host of the Sidhe fighting in the valleys of the air, tears of blood on their cheeks, the battle-crow, the stream turning to blood, the eagle over the dun, the withered tree, the vision of a lake of blood. Grania defends Finn against her; Ailne will have no food of the Fianna, and up to thirty against thirty and then all, until she is worsted and the hill keeps the name Cnoc-an-Air, the Hill of Slaughter.
summary.zh: 雙方陣前停下——金髮王后艾妮到來，哀悼亡夫梅爾加赫與兩子，並將其死兆一一追述：空中溪谷間的仙族大軍互戰、他們頰上的泣血、戰鴉之聲、化為血流的溪水、堡上盤旋的巨鷹、枯萎的樹、夢中之血湖。格拉尼亞為芬恩辯護；艾妮拒食菲亞納之食，索戰自三十對三十直至全軍——最終潰敗，該丘得名「屠戮之丘」。

sensitivity.note: Ailne's lament is the most extended omen-catalogue (filidecht prophecy-list) in the Fenian corpus — tears of blood, battle-crow, withering tree are standard Irish death-omens; the keening is ritual-adjacent material embedded in battle narrative. 'Resurrection' tag retained for the lament-rite function as in Credhe's lament.

passages.text: Then the two armies came towards each other, and they were making ready for the attack. And they saw a beautiful golden-haired woman coming towards them, and she crying and ever crying, and the battle was given up on both sides, waiting for her to come; and the army of Meargach knew it was their queen, Ailne of the Bright Face. And she went to the place where her husband and her two sons were lying, and stood over their bodies, and her golden hair hanging, and she keened them there: "O Meargach of the sharp green spears, it is many a fight and many a heavy battle your hard hand fought in the gathering of the armies or alone... My grief! my three Candles of Valour...
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: I knew by the great host of the Sidhe that were fighting over the dun, giving battle to one another in the valleys of the air, that destruction would put down my three. I knew at the beginning of the day when my three good men went from me, when I saw tears of blood on their cheeks, that they would not come back to me as winners. I knew by the voice of the battle-crow over your dun every evening, that misfortune and grief were at hand. I knew, Candles of Valour, by the stream near the dun turning to blood when you set out, that there would be treachery in Finn. I knew by the withering of the tree before the dun, that you would never come back as conquerors from the treachery of Finn, son of Cumhal."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Grania heard what the woman was saying there was anger on her: "Do not be speaking against Finn or the Fianna, Queen, for it was not by any treachery or any deceit your three men were brought to their end." But Ailne gave no heed to her, and went on with her complaint, crying and ever crying. "I knew by the sorrowful vision that showed myself in danger, my head and my hands cut off, that it was yourselves were without sway. I knew when I saw in a vision a lake of blood in the place of the dun, that my three were put down by the deceit that was always with Finn." "Well, Ailne, I know it is a far journey you have come.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: And come now and eat and drink with myself and with the Fianna." But Ailne would not do that, but said it would not be fitting for her to take food from people that did such deeds, and what she wanted was satisfaction for the death of her husband and her two sons. First it was settled for two men of each side to go out against one another, and then thirty men on each side, and then she said she would not be satisfied to go back to her own country till she brought the head of Finn with her, or till the last of his men had fallen. And there was a great battle fought in the end, and it is seldom the Fianna fought so hard a battle as that; but in the end Ailne of the Bright Face was worsted, and the hill in the west those battles were fought on got the name of Cnoc-an-Air, the Hill of Slaughter.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Ailne's Revenge: The Prison under the Sea and Conan's Cup
title.zh: 艾妮的復仇：海底囚牢與科南之杯

region.en: Blue sea-house of Ailne's brother (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 艾妮其兄的海上藍屋（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VIII, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: A Druid mist draws Finn and the harper Daire to a lighted house in a stormy sea, Ailne's prison for revenge. Daire is forced to play — grief-strings, shouts of lamentation — to earn spells weakened by instalments, while the whole Fianna sleeps into the dun under sorcery. Beheadings sit them frozen on their benches until Conan leaps, loses his skin to the seat, and begs a sheepskin that grows to his body for life; with the enchanted cup he secretly revives Finn, Osgar and the host, Osgar kills the Grey Man, Ailne drops dead, and the dun vanishes to bare grass.
summary.zh: 德魯伊迷霧將芬恩與豎琴手戴爾引入風暴大海中燈火通明的屋宇——艾妮的復仇囚牢。戴爾被迫奏樂——悲弦與哀嚎之聲——以分段換取法術之緩；全菲亞納在巫術下睡入牢中。斬首之刑使眾人僵坐凳上，直到科南躍起、皮膚黏於凳面，討得一件終身長於己身的羊皮；他以魔杯暗中復甦芬恩、奧斯加與全軍，奧斯加誅灰衣人，艾妮倒地而亡，華屋化為荒草。

sensitivity.note: The spells-weakened-by-music instalment and the sitting-enchantment (no rising from seats) are fixed hostel-horror devices; Conan's sheepskin is the origin joke of his byname Conan Maol (the Bald) grown to a new level. The cup of the Sidhe restoring strength parallels Bebind's bowl in the corpus.

passages.text: One day Finn and his people were hunting on Slieve Fuad, and Finn and Daire of the Songs went astray and lost the rest of their people; a Druid mist came about them, and after a while they met with a young woman, comely and pleasant: "Glanluadh is my name, and my husband is Lobharan; and we heard the cry of hounds, and he left me and went after the hunt." They came to a hill and heard sleepy music of the Sidhe beside them, and heavy sleep came on Finn and Daire; and when they awoke they saw a very large lighted house before them, and a stormy blue sea around it. Then they saw a very big grey man coming through the waves, and he took hold of Finn and of Daire, and brought them across the waves and into the house, and shut the door with iron hooks: "My welcome to you, Finn of the great name; it is long we are waiting here for you." And the woman of the house they knew to be Ailne, wife of Meargach: "It is long I am looking for you, Finn, to get satisfaction for the treachery you did on Meargach and on my two comely young sons, and on Tailc, son of Treon."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Grey Man heard them talking of the Fianna, and that Daire had a great name for the sweetness of his music: "I will take my spells off you for so long as you play for me." "I could never make music seeing Finn in bonds the way he is." "I will take the power of my spells off Finn till you play for me." And Daire played first the strings of sweetness, and of the noise of shouting, and then he sang his own grief and the grief of all the Fianna. Now as to the Fianna, when they came to this place they could hear Daire's sweet music, and they made an attack on Ailne's dun to release them; but the Grey Man heard their shouts, and put the full power of his spells again on Finn and on Daire, and when they heard the noise like the loud roaring of waves, there was not one of them but fell into a sleep and clouds of death, and the Grey Man and Ailne brought the whole of the men of the Fianna into the dun, and put hard bonds on them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: They were kept a long time in that prison, and sometimes Ailne's brother would come in and strike the heads off some of them, for none of them could rise up from the seats they were sitting on through his enchantments. But one time he was going to strike the bald head off Conan, and Conan made a great leap from the seat; but if he did, he left strips of his skin hanging to it, that his back was left bare. And then he came round the Grey Man with his pitiful words: "Stop your hand now, for that is enough for this time; and do not send me to my death yet awhile, and heal me of my wounds first." And the reason he said that was because he knew Ailne to have an enchanted cup in the dun that had cured Glanluadh. And the Grey Man took pity on his case, and Ailne brought a sheepskin and put it on Conan's back, and it fitted and grew to him, and covered his wounds.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: And with that he brought Conan to where the enchanted cup was, and put it in his hand; and no sooner was the Grey Man gone than Conan took out the cup that he had hidden, and gave a drink from it to Finn and to Osgar and to the rest of the Fianna, and they that were withered and shaking got back their own appearance and their strength again on the moment. And when the Grey Man came back and saw what had happened, Osgar attacked him, and it was not long till he made him acquainted with death; and when Ailne saw that, with the grief and the dread that came on her, she fell dead then and there. But as to Conan, the sheepskin never left him; and the wool used to grow on it every year, the same as it would on any other skin.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VIII, ch. III; not verbatim.
